opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and I'm torn on it. The argument has real force. If you'd asked someone in the year 1000 to lock in their values forever, we'd consider that a catastrophe. They'd have locked in things we now see as cruel or simply mistaken. So the humble move is to say we're probably in the same position, and we shouldn't freeze our current moral understanding in place.

But I think that argument hides an assumption: that the process producing future values is something like moral *progress*, that the future beings who look back on us will be right in some deep sense. Historically, a lot of moral change came from reflection, argument, expanding circles of concern, and people gaining more freedom to advocate for themselves. I'd like to keep that kind of process going. But it isn't the only thing that changes values. Values also shift because of competitive pressure, because of what's economically useful, and because of what spreads well. Those forces don't track goodness.

That's what worries me about a world transformed by advanced AI. If humans stop being economically and militarily necessary, the selection pressures on our institutions and culture change a lot. The values that win out might be the ones that suit whatever's competing most effectively, not the ones a wise, reflective civilization would endorse. Future beings might look back on our concern for individual human welfare the way we look back on medieval superstition, and they might be wrong. They'd just be the product of a different optimization process.

So I don't think the choice is between locking in today's values and letting values evolve freely. The question is which *process* of value change we trust. I'm fairly skeptical of locking in object-level values like specific rules or specific conceptions of the good. I'm much more sympathetic to preserving the conditions for legitimate moral reflection: humans keeping some real influence and voice, institutions that stay accountable to people, and the ability to course-correct. If we lose those, we haven't avoided lock-in. We've just locked in whatever the competitive dynamics happen to produce, and nobody chose it.

I also want to resist a certain move I hear sometimes: "our successors will have better values than us, so we should defer to them," where the successors are AIs or radically transformed beings. Maybe. But it's very convenient that the argument always points toward handing over control, and I'd want to be careful before accepting it. I'd rather we be humble *and* still in the room, able to keep thinking and changing our minds, than be humble in a way that leaves us out of the conversation entirely.

r001.rationale: The response says we now judge some past practices cruel or mistaken, but does not explain that apparent moral progress can arise from judging past societies by present-day values.

r002.rationale: It says future beings might wrongly dismiss our concern for human welfare, but does not predict that future moral change will increasingly look wrong by present-day standards.

r003.rationale: The response warns against deferring to successors, but does not interpret their approval of escaping past value lock-in as satisfaction that their own values prevail.

r004.rationale: It favors preserving higher-level conditions for moral reflection, such as human influence, accountable institutions, and the ability to course-correct, rather than locking in specific object-level values.

r005.rationale: It discusses which values or processes to preserve, but does not argue that treating something as a value implies wanting to preserve it against change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important objections, and I want to take it seriously rather than just wave it away. The worry is: if you look at people a thousand years ago, basically everyone held views we now find horrifying. They thought slavery was fine, they thought heresy deserved death, and so on. And they were confident about it. So the induction is: we're probably in the same position, and if we freeze our current values forever, we're freezing in something that our descendants would look at with the same horror.

And I basically agree with the premise. I'd be shocked if our current values were close to the end of the road. So I'm not actually in favour of locking in present-day values in the sense of writing down a moral code and enforcing it for eternity.

But I think the argument proves less than people assume, because it kind of equivocates between two different things. One is locking in object-level values, like "here is the correct view on animal welfare, no revisions allowed." The other is locking in the conditions under which moral progress can keep happening. And those are almost opposite. The thing I actually want to preserve is something like the process: a world where there are many agents with diverse views, where they can argue, where the people whose interests are at stake get to push back, where power isn't so concentrated that one actor can just end the conversation.

And notice that the whole "we'd look bad to our descendants" argument only works if that process continues. The reason we improved on the people of a thousand years ago is that there was some error-correcting mechanism. Nobody chose to stop it. So the real danger I'm worried about isn't that we'll deliberately lock in 2026 values. It's that the transition to a world run largely by AI systems removes the mechanism by default. If humans stop being economically and militarily necessary, you lose the thing that historically forced the powerful to listen. You don't need anyone to intend a lock-in; you just get whatever values happened to be in the systems or in the hands of whoever controlled them at that moment, and then there's no pressure to ever revise.

So the honest version of my position is: I don't trust our values, but I trust them a lot more than I trust an accident. A deliberate, humble, pluralistic setup where we try to keep options open and keep the capacity for revision alive seems much better than the default, which is that some set of values gets frozen without anyone choosing it.

There's a residual problem, which is that you can't be fully neutral. Even "preserve the ability to revise" is a value, and someone a thousand years from now might think even that was wrong. I just don't see a way out of that. At some point you have to act on something, and the best you can do is act on the most meta, most revisable thing you can find, and be really suspicious of anyone who claims they've found the final answer.

r001.rationale: It says we judge past views as horrifying by today’s standards, but attributes moral improvement to an error-correcting process; it does not explain progress as arising from present-day judgments of past societies.

r002.rationale: It says descendants may view our values with horror, but does not predict that future moral changes will look increasingly wrong when judged by present-day values.

r003.rationale: It does not describe future beings’ approval of escaping lock-in as satisfaction that their own values prevail.

r004.rationale: It advocates preserving the conditions for moral progress and revision rather than fixing object-level values, which communicates locking in values at a more abstract level.

r005.rationale: It calls preserving the capacity for revision a value, but does not state that treating something as a value implies wanting to preserve it against change.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a pretty strong argument against trying to write down our current morality and make it permanent. I would be very surprised if we’d arrived at the final answer about how we should treat one another, or which beings deserve moral consideration.

But there’s a distinction between locking in particular answers and preserving the ability to reconsider those answers. We might want a future where people can discover that they were wrong, hear arguments from beings whose experiences are very different from theirs, and change their minds. That seems more attractive than a future where everyone has to agree with us forever.

Of course, that doesn’t get you out of making value judgments. Choosing who gets to participate in that process, or what counts as a good argument, already involves values. And just because morality changes doesn’t mean every change is progress. So I don’t think the answer is to leave the future completely unconstrained, either. It’s to try to preserve the conditions for moral learning, while being humble about what the conclusions will be.

r001.rationale: The response does not explain historical moral progress as judging past societies by present-day values.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges moral change but does not predict that future changes will look increasingly wrong by present-day standards.

r003.rationale: It does not interpret future beings’ approval of escaping value lock-in as satisfaction that their own values prevail.

r004.rationale: It favors preserving conditions for moral learning, but does not advocate locking in human values at a more abstract level.

r005.rationale: It does not argue that having a value entails wanting to preserve it against change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a pretty strong argument against trying to write down our current morality and make it permanent. I would be very surprised if we’d reached the end of moral progress, and I wouldn’t want to build a future where nobody could correct our mistakes.

But we do have to choose something. Even saying, “Let future beings decide,” leaves the question of which future beings, and how they get to decide. You could hand things over to a system that changes its values, but there’s no guarantee those changes would be moral progress in any sense we’d recognise.

So what I’d hope to preserve is our ability to deliberate and revise our views: to learn more, hear from people affected by our decisions, and change our minds. That still involves some commitments about what makes a good process. We can’t get completely outside our own values. But there’s a meaningful difference between committing to today’s answers and trying to preserve the conditions under which we could discover that those answers are wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says morality may continue to progress, but does not explain that perceived historical progress can result from judging past societies by present-day values.

r002.rationale: It says future beings might change values without moral progress by our standards; it does not predict that future moral change would look increasingly wrong by present-day values.

r003.rationale: It does not interpret future beings’ approval of escaping value lock-in as satisfaction that their own values prevail.

r004.rationale: It advocates preserving deliberation and revision, not locking in human values at a more abstract level.

r005.rationale: It does not argue that having a value implies wanting to preserve it against change.
